subject: physics

items.q: Which of these is closest to the radius of a typical atom?
items.correct: About 1 x 10^-10 m, a ten-billionth of a metre
items.misconception: About 1 x 10^-15 m, the size of a nucleus
items.why: Two very small powers of ten are learned in the same lesson and students remember the smaller one as the more impressive 'atom' figure. Anchor the atom first: atom about 1 x 10^-10 m. The nucleus is smaller by a factor of more than 10 000, which lands near 10^-15 m.
items.random_wrong: About 1 x 10^-6 m, a thousandth of a mm

items.q: Which statement describes the basic structure of an atom?
items.correct: A positive nucleus of protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons
items.misconception: A positive nucleus of protons and electrons, with neutrons outside
items.why: Students know the nucleus is where the charge is, and reason that both charged particles must therefore live there. Only protons and neutrons sit in the nucleus. Electrons are arranged at different distances from the nucleus, outside it.
items.random_wrong: A negative nucleus of protons and neutrons, with electrons outside it

items.q: How does the radius of a nucleus compare with the radius of the atom?
items.correct: It is less than 1/10 000 of the atom's radius
items.misconception: It is about 1/10 of the atom's radius, as pictured
items.why: Every textbook diagram has to draw the nucleus big enough to see. Students read those pictures as scale drawings. Scale it up: if an atom were a sports stadium, the nucleus would be a pea on the centre spot. Volume goes as radius cubed, so under 1/10 000 of the radius means under 1/10^12 of the volume.
items.random_wrong: It is roughly 1/100 of the atom's radius in all atoms

items.q: Where is nearly all of the mass of an atom found?
items.correct: In the nucleus, in the protons and neutrons
items.misconception: In the electrons, because there are so many of them
items.why: Volume is confused with mass: electrons occupy nearly all of the space, so students assume they contribute nearly all of the substance. Mass and volume are separate. Electrons occupy almost all the volume but almost none of the mass; the protons and neutrons hold it.
items.random_wrong: Spread out evenly throughout the atom's volume

items.q: An electron in an atom absorbs electromagnetic radiation. What happens to that electron?
items.correct: It moves further from the nucleus, to a higher energy level
items.misconception: It moves closer to the nucleus, to a lower energy level
items.why: 'Absorb' sounds like being drawn in, and students picture the electron being sucked towards the centre. Energy in means the electron is lifted away from the attraction of the nucleus: further out is a higher energy level. Emission is the reverse.
items.random_wrong: It escapes the atom, leaving behind a positive ion

items.q: An atom emits electromagnetic radiation. What has one of its electrons done?
items.correct: Moved closer to the nucleus, to a lower energy level
items.misconception: Moved further from the nucleus, to a higher energy level
items.why: 'Absorb' sounds like being drawn in, and students picture the electron being sucked towards the centre. Energy in means the electron is lifted away from the attraction of the nucleus: further out is a higher energy level. Emission is the reverse.
items.random_wrong: Left the atom, carrying the energy away with it

items.q: Why does an atom have no overall electrical charge?
items.correct: It has equal numbers of protons and electrons
items.misconception: Its neutrons cancel out the charge of the protons
items.why: The name 'neutron' sounds like the thing that makes the atom neutral, so students give it that job. Neutrons have no charge at all, so they cannot cancel anything. Neutrality comes from equal numbers of protons and electrons.
items.random_wrong: It has just as many electrons as it has neutrons

items.q: What is the atomic number of an element?
items.correct: The number of protons in the nucleus
items.misconception: The number of protons and neutrons added
items.why: Both numbers appear in the same symbol and both are described as 'numbers of particles in the nucleus'. Atomic number is protons only. Protons plus neutrons is the mass number, the larger figure written above it.
items.random_wrong: The number of electrons in the outer shell

items.q: What does the mass number of an atom tell you?
items.correct: The total number of protons and neutrons in the atom
items.misconception: The number of neutrons in the nucleus of the atom
items.why: Isotopes differ in mass number and in neutrons, so students conclude the mass number is a neutron count. Mass number is protons plus neutrons. Neutron number is what is left after subtracting the atomic number.
items.random_wrong: The number of protons and electrons in the atom

items.q: An atom of sodium has mass number 23 and atomic number 11. How many neutrons are in its nucleus?
items.correct: 12 neutrons, worked out from 23 - 11 = 12
items.misconception: 11 neutrons, since 11 is the smaller number
items.why: The two words look and sound alike, and both particles are counted from the nuclear symbol. Match electrons to protons, because those are the two charged particles. Neutron number is mass number minus atomic number.
items.random_wrong: 34 neutrons, found from 23 + 11 = 34

items.q: In the conventional representation of an atom, what does the lower number stand for?
items.correct: The atomic number, which counts the protons
items.misconception: The mass number, the protons plus the neutrons
items.why: Periodic table entries vary in layout, and 'atomic' feels like the more important label, so it is put first. The larger of the two numbers is always the mass number, and it sits above the atomic number. For sodium: 23 above 11.
items.random_wrong: The number of neutrons found inside the nucleus

items.q: What are isotopes of an element?
items.correct: Atoms with equal protons, unequal neutrons
items.misconception: Atoms which have different numbers of protons
items.why: Any change to the nucleus gets attributed to protons, the particle students think of first. Change the protons and you change the element. Isotopes of one element must all have the same number of protons.
items.random_wrong: Atoms of the element that have lost an electron

items.q: How does an atom turn into a positive ion?
items.correct: By losing one or more electrons from its outer shell
items.misconception: By gaining one or more electrons from elsewhere
items.why: 'Losing' is read as 'becoming less', and students attach that to the sign of the charge instead of to the negative particles. Count the charges: remove a negative electron and the positives left over win, so the ion is positive.
items.random_wrong: By gaining one extra proton into its nucleus

items.q: Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 are isotopes. Which statement about them is correct?
items.correct: They have the same atomic number but different mass numbers
items.misconception: They have different atomic numbers and different mass numbers
items.why: Any change to the nucleus gets attributed to protons, the particle students think of first. Change the protons and you change the element. Isotopes of one element must all have the same number of protons.
items.random_wrong: They have the same mass number but a different charge

items.q: A lithium atom with mass number 7 and atomic number 3 loses one electron. What is the resulting ion?
items.correct: Charge +1, mass number is still 7, 3 protons
items.misconception: Charge -1, because one electron has been removed
items.why: 'Losing' is read as 'becoming less', and students attach that to the sign of the charge instead of to the negative particles. Count the charges: remove a negative electron and the positives left over win, so the ion is positive.
items.random_wrong: Charge +1, mass number 6, with 3 protons still

items.q: What should happen to an accepted scientific model when new experimental evidence does not fit it?
items.correct: The model is changed or is replaced
items.misconception: The model is kept, since it is proved
items.why: School science is met as settled fact, so 'accepted' is heard as 'proved for good'. The atom is the standard example: sphere, then plum pudding, then nuclear, then Bohr, each changed by new evidence.
items.random_wrong: The evidence is put down to an error

items.q: How were atoms described before the discovery of the electron?
items.correct: As tiny spheres that could not be divided at all
items.misconception: As tiny spheres with a nucleus at their centre
items.why: The modern picture is so familiar that students cannot imagine a model without a nucleus in it. The nucleus only arrived after the scattering experiment, which was years after the electron. Before the electron the atom was indivisible.
items.random_wrong: As balls of positive charge full of electrons

items.q: What did the plum pudding model suggest about the atom?
items.correct: The atom is a ball of positive charge with electrons in it
items.misconception: The atom has a small positive nucleus with electrons orbiting
items.why: Only one atomic picture is remembered clearly, and the label is attached to whichever model is described. Plum pudding has no nucleus at all: the positive charge is spread through the whole ball, with electrons stuck in it.
items.random_wrong: The atom is a ball of negative charge with protons in it

items.q: In the alpha particle scattering experiment, what happened to most of the alpha particles?
items.correct: They passed straight through the metal foil
items.misconception: They bounced straight back from the metal foil
items.why: The surprising result is the memorable one, so the rare event is remembered as the usual one. The evidence has two halves: most passing through shows the atom is mostly empty; a few deflected shows a tiny dense charged centre.
items.random_wrong: They were deflected by exactly the same angle

items.q: What is the key difference between the plum pudding model and the nuclear model?
items.correct: The nuclear model puts the charge at the centre
items.misconception: The nuclear model has the electrons embedded in charge
items.why: The two models are learned as a pair and the descriptions are matched to the wrong names under exam pressure. Nuclear model: tiny charged centre, electrons outside. Plum pudding: charge spread out, electrons embedded within it.
items.random_wrong: The plum pudding model has a nucleus at its centre

items.q: What did Niels Bohr add to the nuclear model of the atom?
items.correct: Electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances only
items.misconception: Electrons may orbit the nucleus at any distance
items.why: The planetary picture of the atom carries over from gravity, where any orbit radius is possible. Bohr's contribution was exactly this: electrons orbit at specific distances, and his calculations then agreed with observation.
items.random_wrong: The nucleus lies at the centre and holds the mass

items.q: Later experiments showed that the positive charge of any nucleus could be subdivided. What followed from this?
items.correct: The proton was named, each carrying equal positive charge
items.misconception: The nuclear charge was shown to be a single indivisible lump
items.why: The nucleus is drawn as a single blob, and the early nuclear model did treat its charge as one quantity. Later experiments showed the charge comes in equal whole units. Each unit is a proton, so nuclear charge is a whole number of them.
items.random_wrong: The neutron was named, a particle carrying no charge

items.q: What did the experimental work of James Chadwick provide evidence for?
items.correct: The existence of neutrons within the nucleus
items.misconception: The existence of a nucleus in every atom
items.why: The three nuclear discoveries are listed together and the names get attached to the wrong particle. Chadwick's evidence was for the neutron, about 20 years after the nucleus had become an accepted scientific idea.
items.random_wrong: The existence of protons inside all atomic nuclei

items.q: Why did the scattering experiment lead scientists to change the model of the atom?
items.correct: A few alpha particles bounced back, which the old model forbade
items.misconception: Scientists preferred the newer picture because it was simpler to draw
items.why: Students know models change, but not that evidence is what forces the change, so they reach for convenience instead. A model is only replaced when observations defeat it. Alpha particles deflected backwards are impossible in a plum pudding atom.
items.random_wrong: Every alpha particle bounced back, showing the atom is solid all through

items.q: Is the mass of an atom spread out evenly?
items.correct: No. Most of the mass of an atom is concentrated in the nucleus at the centre.
items.misconception: The mass is spread evenly through the sphere of the atom, like the mass of a marble.
items.why: Atoms are drawn as filled circles, and everyday solid objects do have evenly spread mass. The scattering experiment is exactly the evidence against this: an evenly spread atom could not deflect an alpha particle backwards.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does absorbing or emitting radiation remove the electron from the atom?
items.correct: No. The electron changes energy level; it moves further from or closer to the nucleus but stays in the atom.
items.misconception: Absorbing radiation throws the electron out of the atom, and emitting radiation is the electron leaving.
items.why: Ionisation is met in the same topic, so any electron movement gets read as the electron escaping. Changing energy level is a move between allowed distances inside the atom. Losing an electron altogether is ionisation, a different event.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the atomic number tell you about the outer electrons?
items.correct: The atomic number is the number of protons; in a neutral atom that equals the total number of electrons, not the outer ones.
items.misconception: The atomic number is the number of electrons in the outer shell of the atom.
items.why: Chemistry lessons stress outer-shell electrons and group number, and the two 'numbers' get merged. Group number relates to outer electrons; atomic number counts protons, and therefore all the electrons in a neutral atom.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How do you get the number of neutrons from the symbol?
items.correct: Subtract the atomic number from the mass number.
items.misconception: Add the two numbers together to find the neutrons.
items.why: Students remember that the mass number involves combining particles and apply the addition in the wrong direction. Mass number = protons + neutrons, so neutrons = mass number - atomic number. For sodium, 23 - 11 = 12 neutrons.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are isotopes atoms that have gained or lost electrons?
items.correct: No. Isotopes have different numbers of neutrons; their electron numbers are the same.
items.misconception: Isotopes are atoms of an element that have gained or lost electrons.
items.why: Isotopes and ions are taught together as 'atoms that are not standard', and the two definitions get swapped. Electrons change gives an ion, with a charge. Neutrons change gives an isotope, with a different mass number and no charge.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can an atom become a positive ion by gaining a proton?
items.correct: No. Atoms turn into positive ions by losing one or more outer electrons.
items.misconception: An atom becomes positive when an extra proton joins its nucleus.
items.why: It looks like the direct route to a positive charge, and students forget that changing the protons changes the element. Adding a proton would make a different element altogether. Ion formation only moves outer electrons.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the mass number change when an atom forms an ion?
items.correct: No. Losing an electron changes the charge but leaves the mass number unchanged.
items.misconception: The mass number falls by one for each electron lost.
items.why: Any particle leaving seems as though it must reduce the mass, and 'mass number' invites that reasoning. Mass number counts only protons and neutrons. An electron's mass is negligible and it is not counted, so 23 stays 23.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When did the plum pudding model appear?
items.correct: After the discovery of the electron, which is what the model was invented to accommodate.
items.misconception: Before the electron was discovered, as the earliest picture of the atom.
items.why: The plum pudding model feels primitive, so it is filed as the very first idea about atoms. The model needs electrons in it, so it cannot pre-date them. Order: indivisible sphere, then plum pudding, then nuclear.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Were the alpha particles all deflected in the same way?
items.correct: No. Most were not deflected at all, and only a small number were deflected through large angles.
items.misconception: Every alpha particle was deflected by about the same angle as it went through.
items.why: A uniform result is what most school experiments give, so students expect consistency here too. A uniform deflection would suggest evenly spread charge. It is the mixture of outcomes that points to a tiny nucleus.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What did Niels Bohr contribute?
items.correct: He adapted the nuclear model by suggesting that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances.
items.misconception: He proposed the nuclear model itself, by discovering that the atom has a nucleus.
items.why: Bohr's name is attached to the familiar orbit diagram, which students take to be the whole nuclear model. The nucleus came from the scattering experiment. Bohr's addition was the specific allowed distances, which matched calculation.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In a model of the atom, which particles carry the negative charge?
items.correct: The electrons are negative in every model, and whatever they sit in or orbit is positive.
items.misconception: The main body of the atom is negative and the electrons embedded in it are positive.
items.why: The signs are memorised as labels on a picture, and the picture is recalled without them, so the pair gets flipped. Fix one sign and the rest follows: electrons are always negative, so whatever they sit in, or orbit, must be positive.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How small is 'very small' for an atom?
items.correct: About 1 x 10^-10 m, far too small to be seen with any light microscope.
items.misconception: About a millimetre, which is the smallest length marked on a ruler.
items.why: 'Very small' is judged against everyday experience, and the smallest length a student can actually point at is a millimetre division. A millimetre is 1 x 10^-3 m, and about ten million atoms would fit across it. An atom is about 1 x 10^-10 m.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which particles does the mass number count?
items.correct: Protons and neutrons only.
items.misconception: Protons and electrons, since those are the two numbers that are equal in an atom.
items.why: The atomic number is linked with electrons in a neutral atom, so students carry the proton-electron pairing over to the mass number as well. Mass number counts only the particles in the nucleus. An electron is about 2000 times lighter than a proton and is not counted.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.4.1 Atoms and isotopes
